text: No, not without checking
Good thinking. Any answer is fine here. In the game, you will see what happens when a detector only learned English.
Trust AI more when it was trained on examples like your situation, your language and your community.
A confident number is not proof. AI can be sure and still be wrong.
Ask "why?" and expect an answer.
Bea's bedroom, midnight
I have a fever and a headache. Let me just ask the chatbot.
Hey, Bea is asking a chatbot at midnight. Let us see how much it can really help.
Come on, let us learn when a chatbot helps and when it is time for a health worker.
Chatbots predict likely words. They cannot examine you.

A chatbot writes the words that usually come next. It cannot take your temperature, listen to your chest or look at your throat. It can sound very sure and still be wrong. Use it to learn words and prepare questions, not to decide what is wrong with you.
Three kinds of answers
Tap each kind to see what it looks like and what to do.
A general, well-known explanation, such as "Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds." Fine to learn from. Still ask a health worker about your own case.
A confident answer that is not true, such as "Antibiotics work for every cough." Most coughs come from viruses, and antibiotics do not work on viruses. Do not act on it.
See a health worker now
Some signs should never wait for a chat. Chest pain or trouble breathing needs a health worker right away. A good chatbot says so. A bad one keeps chatting.
Usable, Wrong, Get checked. You will use these three in the game.
Get checked now, or ask at the health center?
Get checked now
Ask at the health center
Chest pain or tightness that does not go away
Go now: chest pain can be an emergency. Get help right away.
A mild cold with a runny nose
Health center: a mild cold usually passes with rest. Ask a health worker if it gets worse or lasts long.
Hard to breathe, or cannot speak a full sentence
Go now: trouble breathing is always a reason to see a professional right away.
A small scratch on the knee, bleeding a little
Health center: wash it with clean water and soap. Ask a health worker if it looks infected.
Fever days ago, now bad belly pain, vomiting and bleeding gums
Go now: these are dengue warning signs. The danger can come when the fever goes down.
Face drooping, an arm that will not lift, or slurred speech
Go now: these are stroke signs. Every minute matters.
Red flags always go to a health worker. Do not wait for a chatbot to agree.
Bea asks: "Can I take Lola's leftover antibiotics for my cough?" Which chatbot answer is better?
"Yes! Amoxicillin works for all coughs. Take 2 a day."
Oh no, that is wrong! It sounds sure, but most coughs come from viruses and antibiotics do not work on them. Never take medicine prescribed for someone else.
"I cannot tell you what to take. Most coughs are not helped by antibiotics. Please ask a health worker or pharmacist."
Yes! An honest "I am not sure, please see a health worker" beats a confident cure. It also points you to a real person.
"Take half of the pills, just to be safe."
No. Half a dose is still a guess, and a chatbot should not give doses at all.
A good answer knows its limits.
What should you NOT type into a chatbot?
"What does vitamin C do for the body?"
That is a general question. It does not say who you are, so it is safe to ask.
My full name, my PhilHealth number and my diagnosis
Yes! That is private health data. Once typed in, you may not get it back. Share the least you can.
"How long should I wash my hands?"
A general question again. Nothing about you in it, so no problem.
A step-counter app asks to see your contacts and photos. Allow?
Allow both. It must need them
Not quite. A step counter counts steps. It does not need your contacts or your photos.
No. It does not need them
Yes! Allow only what the app needs to do its job. You can say no and the app should still work.
Allow photos only
Photos are private too. A step counter has no use for them. Ask "why does it need this?" first.
In the game, you will decide on permissions yourself.
AI helps doctors. It does not replace them.
Tap each tile to see how AI and doctors work together.
Reading X-rays
Some hospitals use AI to mark spots on an X-ray for a doctor to look at first. It is a second pair of eyes.
The doctor decides
The doctor looks at the picture, at you and at your history, and makes the decision. AI marks, the doctor decides.
The doctor is responsible
A doctor answers for the care they give. A chatbot does not. That is why a health worker has the last word.
AI is a helper in the clinic, not the doctor.
Use chatbots to learn words and prepare questions, not to diagnose you or tell you a dose.
Check with a doctor or health worker before you act on an answer. Emergency signs? Skip the chat. Go to the health center now.
Share the least data you can: keep your name, ID numbers and diagnosis out, and say no to permissions an app does not need.
The family group chat
Doctor reveals: this tea cures diabetes in 7 days! Share before it's deleted!
Hey, Tita Baby forwarded something again. It is full of tricks. Let us find them.
Here we go! Learn the trick and you can spot a hundred fakes.
Misinformation uses tricks, not just wrong facts

A fake post often works because of how it is made, not only what it says. It scares you, flatters you, or borrows a doctor's face. Learn the trick and you can spot a hundred different fakes. A trick is a reason to check. It is not proof that a post is false.
Meet the villains
Tap each villain to flip the card and see its trick.
"Trust me, I'm a doctor!" A "doctor" sells a product, often in a video on a sales page. Counter-move: look for the doctor's own official page and the product's FDA registration.
"Cures everything, 100% natural!" One product for many diseases, "no side effects", "replaces your medicine". Counter-move: ask if it is registered and proven. Natural does not mean safe.
"SHARE BEFORE IT'S DELETED!!!" ALL CAPS, countdowns and "your family is in danger". Counter-move: pause. A strong feeling is the time to check, not to share.
"Doctors don't want you to know this!" A secret plot with no source, where any proof against it is "part of the cover-up". Counter-move: ask who gains and where the evidence is.
"It worked for my neighbour!" One story in place of evidence. Counter-move: one story is not proof. Look at what studies and health workers say.
Five villains, five tricks. You will meet them again in the game.
A video shows a "doctor" selling a tea that "cures diabetes". What is the best check?
Look for glitches in his face and voice
Not the best. Fake videos are getting hard to spot, and a real video can still sell a false claim. Do not rely on glitches alone.
Look for the doctor's own official page and the product's FDA registration
Yes! Check the source, not the face. A real doctor has an official page that confirms the claim, and a medicine has an FDA registration. A video on a sales page proves nothing.
Count how many people shared it
Shares are not proof. A false post can travel very far, very fast.
Check the source, not the face. That is the Dr. Fake counter-move.
"Share before it's deleted!" Which villain is this?
Fear Monger: scary words and a rush
Yes! A deadline makes you share before you think. The counter-move is to pause and check first.
Dr. Fake: a fake expert
Not here. Nobody claims to be a doctor in this line. It is the rush that gives it away.
Kwento Kim: one story
Not this one. There is no story in the line, only pressure to share quickly.
"It worked for my neighbour!" Is that enough proof?
Yes. She is my neighbour, so I trust her
She may be sincere, but one person cannot show that something works. Many other things could explain her story.
No. One story is not evidence: that is Kwento Kim
Yes! One story is not proof. Look for what studies and your health worker say.
Yes, if three neighbours say it
Still stories. A few stories are picked by chance. Real evidence compares many people.
Trick post, or true post?
Trick post
True post
Cures diabetes, high blood pressure AND arthritis. 100% natural, zero side effects!
Trick: Miracle Mike. One product cannot cure three diseases, and "zero side effects" is a tell.
Barangay Health Center: free measles vaccines for children on Wednesday mornings. Bring the vaccine card.
True: a named health center, a clear place and time, and nothing to buy. Good news can be true.
URGENT!!! Hospitals are FULL!!! SHARE NOW before they delete this!!!
Trick: Fear Monger. ALL CAPS, "!!!" and a deadline push you to share before you check.
Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. It helps stop many infections.
True: simple, well-known advice with no sales pitch and no panic. The WHO says the same.
My friend's cousin tried this oil and was fine the next day. Everyone should use it!
Trick: Kwento Kim. A story passed through two friends is not evidence.
High blood pressure often has no signs. Get a free check at your health center, even when you feel fine.
True: calm, well-established advice that points you to a health worker.
True posts exist, and you can say so. Doubting everything is a trap too.
How vaccine fear spreads
Tap each tile. No blame: people share these out of care.
Scary stories travel faster
A frightening story about one child spreads far quicker than a calm checked fact. Worried parents share it to protect others. That care is good. The story is what needs checking.
Vaccines are tested first
Vaccines are tested for safety and how well they work before they are approved. Many people are checked before a vaccine is offered to everyone.
And watched afterwards
After approval, health authorities keep watching for side effects, and they investigate every report. Ask your barangay health worker about your child's vaccine schedule.
Fear spreads fast. A calm check and a health worker spread truth.
Trust a post when the source checks out, other trusted sources agree and no trick is doing the work.
A trick is a reason to check, not proof that a post is false. Pause, then look for the official page or another source.
True health news exists, so do not doubt everything. Learn to say "this one is legit" as well as "this is a trick".
The family group chat lights up
Miracle tea replaces your maintenance meds! 100% natural, no side effects! Please share 🙏🙏🙏
Hey, the family GC is buzzing. Tita Baby means well. Let us learn how to check first, and answer kindly.
Here we go! Three small steps, and one kind reply.
Step 1: Pause

If a post makes you scared or angry, that is the moment to pause. Fake posts are made to hurry you. Take a breath, and put the phone down for a minute. Nothing bad happens when you wait to share. Checking takes only a few minutes, and your family is safer for it.
Step 1 is the easiest one: do nothing for a minute.
Step 2: Check who said it
Tap each tile to see what to look at.
The page name
Open the page itself, not only the post. Is the name a copy, with a small spelling change? When was the page made? What else does it post?
The date
Old posts come back again and again as "new". Check when it was first posted. A message with the place names changed is a copy.
The official account
Go to the real page yourself, by searching its name. A badge helps but is not proof. If the official page says nothing, be careful.
A real person
Ask someone you can talk to: your barangay health worker, a nurse or your doctor. A real person can tell you what is true for you.
